blocks.text: If you lead a team of 10 to 200 people and run several projects at once, you probably know the feeling of a tool that has grown hard to manage. Spreadsheets pile up and deadlines live in different places, so a new teammate needs a long walkthrough before they can find anything.

So in this guide, we're sharing the best project management software for small teams. For each tool you get real starting prices from the vendors and review sites, honest pros and cons, and a plain note on who should skip it.
We also show you how to compare per-user pricing with flat pricing using your own headcount, which most lists leave to you. Here's what you'll get from the guide:

items: A ranked shortlist of seven tools, including Planwise, that you can trial this week.
Pricing taken from vendor pages such as [ClickUp's pricing page](https://clickup.com/pricing) and [Asana's pricing page](https://asana.com/pricing), with the source named each time.
A short how-to-choose section so you can match a tool to your team size, budget and way of working.

sections.h2: How we picked these project management tools for small teams

blocks.text: A small team has different needs than a large company. You want a tool that sets up quickly, costs a fair amount for your headcount, and shows several projects clearly at once, with few steps between signing up and getting your whole team to use it. If you want a refresher before you compare, our [project management basics](https://planwise.example/blog/project-management-basics) guide covers the terms.
We ran every tool through the same set of checks, so you can compare them side by side without guessing.

items: Each tool has a free plan or a free trial, or we say it doesn't.
Each tool lists a starting price per user, or a flat price for the whole team.
Each tool shows which views it offers, such as list, board, calendar, timeline or Gantt.
Each tool includes what reviewers say works well.
Each tool includes what reviewers say is hard or missing.

blocks.text: Where a vendor lists its own prices, we use that page, for example [ClickUp's pricing page](https://clickup.com/pricing) and [Asana's pricing page](https://asana.com/pricing).

Whenever a number appears in this guide, we name where it came from. Prices and plan limits change often, and different sites can list slightly different starting prices for the same tool, so check the vendor page before you commit.

Planwise is on this list too, and we hold it to the same rules as every other tool, including the same level of detail, honest pros and cons, and a line on who should skip it. That way you can judge it the way you judge the rest.
Each section follows the same order so it's easy to scan, and here's how every tool entry runs:

items: A plain sentence on what the tool is and who it serves.
What it does well, with the views and features that matter for small teams.
Pricing from the vendor or a named review source.
Pros and cons stated kindly and plainly.
Who should skip it, so you can rule a tool out quickly.

sections.h2: 1. Planwise: best for team leads running several projects at once

blocks.text: Planwise is a project management software that helps team leads plan and track several projects at once.
Pricing

Check [Planwise pricing](https://planwise.example/pricing) for the current plan names and prices, so you see the exact numbers from our own page. We don't list a price here until it's confirmed, because plan details change.
Who should skip it
If your team needs a feature Planwise doesn't offer, such as a specific built-in tool you already rely on, a different option may fit you better.
If you're not sure, trial Planwise and one other tool on the same real project for a week, then compare how each one felt to use.

sections.h2: 2. ClickUp: best for an all-in-one workspace

blocks.text: ClickUp is a work management software company that brings tasks, docs, chat and AI into one workspace. You can visit [ClickUp](https://clickup.com/) to see how it presents the whole product in one place.

What it does well is keep a lot of project work under one roof. [Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management) lists over a dozen project views as a pro, and [ClickUp](https://clickup.com) says its free plan includes Kanban boards, a calendar view and time tracking.
What ClickUp costs
Here are the plans as listed on [ClickUp's pricing page](https://clickup.com/pricing). Honestly, it helps that the free plan is a real option and not just a short trial.

items: Free Forever costs $0 and includes unlimited tasks and subtasks, plus unlimited free members.
Core costs $9 per user per month when billed yearly.
Business costs $17 per user per month when billed yearly.

blocks.text: The free plan also comes with 60 MB of storage, so check that number against the files your team shares before you rely on it.
What we like
Reviewers point to a few strengths that matter when you run several projects at once. Here's what [Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management) lists as pros:

items: Workload and time log tracking are built in, so you can see where hours go.
A built-in document editor lets people collaborate on a doc in real time.
A dedicated chat interface helps your team talk without leaving the tool.

blocks.text: What to watch for

The same review names two cons. [Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management) says ClickUp can be difficult to master because the platform is so expansive, and that in the Everything view it can be hard to tell who owns what.
Luckily, you can lower that risk by picking a few views to start with and agreeing on who owns each task before you invite the whole team.
Who should skip it

If you want a very small tool that your team can learn in an afternoon, ClickUp may feel like more than you need. Teams that value a short setup over a long feature list will likely be happier with a simpler option from this guide.

Asana is a work management software company that helps teams plan, track and run projects with AI Teammates. You can see its full lineup on the [Asana site](https://asana.com/), and its pricing page lays out what each plan includes.
Cloudwards lists Asana as best for usability, with a [4.3 rating](https://www.cloudwards.net/).
What it does well

Asana gives every plan the same core ways to look at work. The [Personal plan](https://asana.com/pricing) includes list, board and calendar views, so you can flip between details, flow and deadlines without losing context.
When you move up to Starter, you also get timeline and Gantt views. Honestly, that is the point where Asana starts to feel built for teams that run several projects at once.
What it costs
Here are the prices from [Asana's pricing page](https://asana.com/pricing), along with what each plan adds:

rows: List, board and calendar views, unlimited tasks and projects
$10.99 per user per month, billed annually
Timeline and Gantt views, forms, unlimited automations and reporting dashboards
$24.99 per user per month, billed annually

blocks.text: Portfolios, goals and resource management sit in the top tier. If you need to see who has capacity, plan for the Advanced price from the start.
Who should skip it
Asana may not be the right fit in two cases, and it helps to know them before you start a trial:

items: Your team has three or more people and needs to stay on a free plan, because the [Personal plan](https://asana.com/pricing) covers only 2 users.
You need resource management but would rather not pay the Advanced price, since [Asana lists it in that plan](https://asana.com/pricing).

blocks.text: If neither case describes you, Asana is a strong candidate to trial on one real project, so you can see how its views and plan steps fit your own team.

sections.h2: 4. monday.com: best for visual project tracking

blocks.text: [monday.com](https://monday.com/) is a work management platform that helps teams build workflows, automate manual work and use AI agents.
Here's how Sonary describes it: [visual boards, custom dashboards for project tracking, 200+ templates and 40+ integrations including Zoom](https://sonary.com/project-management).
What it does well
If you want to see several projects at a glance, the dashboards and boards are the main reason to look at monday.com. The template library also gives you a starting point for new work.

items: You get visual boards that show where each project stands.
Custom dashboards let you track progress across projects in one place.
More than 200 templates give you a quick way to set up new work, per [Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management).
More than 40 integrations, including Zoom, connect it to tools your team already uses, per [Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management).
A free mobile app lets you check work away from your desk.

blocks.text: What it costs

Sonary lists a starting price of [$9 per user per month with a 14-day free trial](https://sonary.com/project-management). The best way to judge it is to use that trial on one real project, and you can check the vendor's pricing page for the current plan details before you commit.
Pros and cons
Cloudwards also names it the [best overall project management software, with a 4.35 rating](https://www.cloudwards.net/).
On the other side, Sonary notes that [the help and support area could offer more options and that there is no multilingual support](https://sonary.com/project-management).
Who should skip it

If your team needs the tool and its support in several languages, check that need before you start a trial, since Sonary lists no multilingual support. For everyone else, it's a good candidate for a one-week trial on a live project.

sections.h2: 5. Teamhub: best for one flat price

blocks.text: [Teamhub](https://teamhub.com/) is a software company that puts projects, chat and docs in a single platform.
Here's how it works in practice.
What it does well
You can [see your tasks in six views](https://teamhub.com/), which gives each person a way to look at work that suits them:

items: Kanban view for moving tasks across columns.
Table view and List view for scanning details quickly.
People view for seeing who has what.
Calendar view for deadlines.
Gantt view for timelines.

blocks.text: Chat sits at the center of the product, and Teamhub lets you [convert a comment to a task in one click](https://teamhub.com/). That means a decision made in a conversation can land on your project board without anyone retyping it.
What it costs
Teamhub lists [$99 per month for unlimited users](https://teamhub.com/), and you can start a free trial with no credit card.

To compare this with per-user pricing, multiply a tool's per-user price by your own headcount. For example, a plan at $10.99 per user per month for 10 people comes to about $110 a month, while the same plan for 25 people is about $275.

Run that math with your real team size and with the plan tier you would actually need. Surprisingly, the answer changes quickly as your team grows, so it helps to check it once now and again when you hire.
Moving over from another tool

Teamhub says it will [migrate your data free of charge](https://teamhub.com/) whether you use Asana, ClickUp or Trello, or keep everything in local Excel files. That lowers the effort of a trial, since you can test it with your real projects instead of a blank workspace.
Who should skip it

If your team is very small, a per-user plan may cost you less than $99 a month, so check your own numbers first. Teams that want a long list of outside reviews may also want to look elsewhere, because the Teamhub page we reviewed only shows testimonials from its own customers.

sections.h2: 6. Zoho Projects: best for budget-conscious teams

blocks.text: Zoho Projects is a project management software that helps teams run projects with time tracking and budgeting.
What it does well
Sonary describes Zoho Projects as a [simple application to use](https://sonary.com/project-management), which matters when you want your team working in it quickly.
Sonary also notes that you can set up project budgeting, so you can watch spend next to your tasks instead of in a separate spreadsheet.
What it costs

Sonary lists a [free plan with a starting price of $0 per month](https://sonary.com/project-management). We haven't confirmed the paid plan prices, so check Zoho's own pricing page before you budget for more than the free tier.
Pros and cons
Here's how Sonary's review sums up the good and the trade-offs:

items: Sonary reviewers say the [help documents cover every aspect of the application](https://sonary.com/project-management), which makes it easier for new teammates to learn on their own.
Sonary reviewers like that time tracking, invoicing integrations and budgeting sit in one place.
Sonary says [many features have been removed to encourage subscriptions to Zoho's other products](https://sonary.com/project-management), so you may find yourself looking at extra tools.
Sonary also describes the interface as bland compared with similar products.

blocks.text: Who should skip it

If you want every feature inside one product and don't plan to use other Zoho tools, you may run into those removed features. In that case, a tool that keeps more in a single plan may suit you better.
Luckily, you can test the fit at no cost, so try the free plan on one real project and see whether the simpler look works for your team.

sections.h2: 7. Wrike: best for complex custom workflows

blocks.text: Wrike is a work management software company that helps teams plan and track projects with custom workflows. Its [Sonary listing](https://sonary.com/project-management) shows grid, Gantt, calendar and card views, plus custom dashboards that give you a quick read on how work is going.
What it costs

[Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management) lists a free plan, with a starting price of $0 per month. We haven't confirmed the paid plan prices, so check Wrike's own pricing page before you budget beyond the free tier.
Pros and cons
Here's how Sonary's reviewers describe the good and the trade-offs:

items: Sonary reviewers say [Wrike offers strong support for all users](https://sonary.com/project-management), and especially for enterprise businesses and applications.
Sonary reviewers say it is easy to integrate other tools with Wrike, which helps if your team already relies on several apps.
Sonary reviewers find it very easy to use, even with the customizable dashboards.
Sonary says [pricing could be better for smaller businesses](https://sonary.com/project-management), so you may want to compare plans against your headcount.
Sonary also says the timer is task-based rather than account-based, and it can be tricky for some people to find.

blocks.text: Who should skip it

If your team runs simple processes and doesn't need custom workflows, Wrike may give you more flexibility than you will use. A lighter tool from earlier in this list could get your team up and running faster.
Try the free plan on one real project, and see whether the custom views match how your team works.

sections.h2: How to choose the right project management software for your small team

blocks.text: Next, pick two or three of the seven tools and test them on real work. Here's how we'd narrow the list for a team of 10 to 200 people running several projects at once.
Match the tool to your team size and budget

Start with price, because it rules tools in or out quickly. [ClickUp's pricing page](https://clickup.com/pricing) lists a Free Forever plan at $0, and [Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management) lists free plans for Zoho Projects and Wrike. [Asana's pricing page](https://asana.com/pricing) says its free Personal plan covers 2 users, so a larger team will need a paid plan.

Paid starting prices on the pages we cited run from $9 per user per month at [ClickUp Core](https://clickup.com/pricing) to $10.99 per user per month at [Asana Starter](https://asana.com/pricing). Teamhub takes a different approach, with [$99 per month for unlimited users](https://teamhub.com/).
Here's how to compare the two pricing styles for your own team:

items: Count the people who would use the tool every week, including part-time contributors.
Multiply that number by the per-user price of each tool, using the yearly billing price where one is listed.
Compare each total with the flat monthly price, and note which plan holds the features you need.
Check which features sit behind higher plans, such as [Asana's resource management and portfolios in Advanced](https://asana.com/pricing), before you settle on a number.

blocks.text: Flat pricing such as Teamhub's tends to favor the larger end of the small-team range, while per-user plans often cost less for a handful of people.
Match the tool to how your team works
Next, think about how your team already plans its work, since each habit points toward a different tool from this list. Which of these sounds most like your week?

items: If you want docs and chat beside your tasks, look at Teamhub, which puts [projects, chat and docs in one platform](https://teamhub.com/), or at ClickUp.

If your team lives in spreadsheets, a spreadsheet-style tool such as Zoho Projects or Wrike may feel closer to what you use today, and both have free plans per [Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management).
If your processes have many steps, look at [Wrike](https://sonary.com/project-management), which Sonary lists for complex custom workflows.

blocks.text: A fair test is to run two tools on one real project for a week before you commit. Write a short project brief first, using our [project brief template](https://planwise.example/templates/project-brief), so both trials start from the same plan and you can compare them side by side.
If your team is growing, our guide to [agile for small teams](https://planwise.example/blog/agile-for-small-teams) shows how to keep that plan light as you add people.
Ready to try it on a real project? See [Planwise pricing](https://planwise.example/pricing) and pick the plan that fits your team.
What is the best project management software for small teams?
The right pick depends on how your team works, so we match each tool to a working style. Planwise is built for team leads who run several projects at once.

items: [ClickUp](https://clickup.com/pricing) suits an all-in-one workspace.
[Asana](https://asana.com/pricing) suits team collaboration.
monday.com suits visual tracking.
Teamhub suits one flat price.
Zoho Projects suits a tight budget.
Wrike suits custom workflows.

blocks.text: Is there free project management software for small teams?
Yes, several tools have a free plan, and each one has limits you should check before you commit.

items: [ClickUp's Free Forever plan](https://clickup.com/pricing) costs $0 with unlimited tasks and free members, though it includes only 60 MB of storage.
[Asana's Personal plan](https://asana.com/pricing) is free for 2 users.
[Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management) lists free plans for Zoho Projects and Wrike.

blocks.text: How much does project management software cost?
On the vendor pages, these are the starting prices we found for paid plans.

items: [ClickUp Core](https://clickup.com/pricing) is $9 per user per month billed yearly.
[Asana Starter](https://asana.com/pricing) is $10.99 per user per month billed annually.
[Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management) lists monday.com from $9 per user per month.
[Teamhub](https://teamhub.com/) charges $99 per month for unlimited users.

blocks.text: To compare a per-user price with a flat price, multiply each per-user price by your own headcount.
Which project management tool is easiest to use?

[Cloudwards](https://www.cloudwards.net/) rates Asana best for usability at 4.3, and [Sonary](https://sonary.com/project-management) reviewers call monday.com easy to navigate. We suggest you trial two tools on one real project before you decide, since your own team will be the best judge.
What is project management software?
For a plain-language primer, read our [project management basics](https://planwise.example/blog/project-management-basics) post.
